<!-- Instructor solution. Same body as w6-clustering-exe.Rmd, with answers. -->

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5)
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)
options(width = 110)
```

The same exercise as the handout, with one possible set of answers. Every
number in the answers comes from the table or chart right above it.

## The data

One row per **customer** of a retailer that sells both online and in its
stores. Columns:

| Column | What it is |
|---|---|
| `CustomerID` | the customer |
| `Age` | age in years |
| `Income` | annual income, in dollars |
| `Online_Spend` | dollars the customer spent online last year |
| `InStore_Spend` | dollars the customer spent in the stores last year |

The retailer wants to know **what kinds of customers it has**, and what to
do with each kind. There is no outcome to predict: this is k-means and PCA,
as in Tuesday's slides.

## Task 1: look at the data

```{r task1}
# load the data (the file must be in the same folder as this Rmd)
df <- fread("customer_clustering_data.csv")

# the first rows of the data
knitr::kable(head(df), format.args = list(big.mark = ","))

# a summary of the four numeric columns: smallest, middle, average, largest
num <- df[, .(Age, Income, Online_Spend, InStore_Spend)]
knitr::kable(data.table(Column   = names(num),
                        Smallest = sapply(num, min),
                        Median   = round(sapply(num, median)),
                        Average  = round(sapply(num, mean)),
                        Largest  = sapply(num, max)),
             format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

- How many customers are there, and what does one row describe?
- Look at the ranges of the four columns. Which column has by far the
  largest numbers? Why does that matter for k-means? (Tuesday's "Watch the
  units" slide.)

**Answer:** 198 customers, one row each. Age runs from 17 to 59, income from
\$23,454 to \$105,041, online spend from \$1 to \$3,475, and in-store spend
from \$147 to \$3,615. **Income** has numbers dozens of times larger than the
spend columns and more than a thousand times larger than age. K-means groups
customers by distance, so two customers \$10,000 apart in income would count
as 10,000 "units" apart, while two customers 30 years apart in age would be
only 30 apart. Left alone, income would decide the clusters.

## Task 2: a first picture

```{r task2}
ggplot(df, aes(x = Online_Spend, y = InStore_Spend)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.7, color = "grey35") +
  labs(title = "Online vs. In-Store Spend, Last Year",
       x = "Online spend ($)", y = "In-store spend ($)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

- How many groups do you see? Describe each one in words.

**Answer:** Three. Top left, customers who spend a lot in the stores and
little online. Bottom, customers who spend mostly online and little in the
stores. Top right, customers who spend a lot in both channels. The two upper
groups touch, so the borders are not perfectly sharp.

## Task 3: standardize, then choose k

```{r task3}
# the four columns we cluster on
feat <- df[, .(Online_Spend, InStore_Spend, Age, Income)]

# standardize: each column becomes (value - its mean) / its standard deviation
X <- scale(feat)
knitr::kable(round(head(X), 2))

# elbow curve: run k-means for k = 2 to 10 and record the within-cluster spread
set.seed(123)
wss <- sapply(2:10, function(k) kmeans(X, centers = k, nstart = 20)$tot.withinss)
elbow <- data.table(k = 2:10, wss = round(wss, 1))
knitr::kable(elbow, col.names = c("k", "Within-cluster spread"))

ggplot(elbow, aes(x = k, y = wss)) +
  geom_line(color = "#990000", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2:10) +
  labs(title = "Total Within-Cluster Sum of Squares vs. k",
       x = "Number of clusters k", y = "Total within-cluster SS") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

- After `scale()`, what does a value of 0 in `X` mean? And a value of 1?
- Where is the elbow? Propose a k, with the numbers from the elbow table.

**Answer:** A 0 is exactly the average customer on that column; a 1 is one
standard deviation above the average (\$19,976 for income, 10 years for age).
Every column is now on the same footing. Going from 2 to 3 clusters cuts the
within-cluster spread from **399 to 181**; going from 3 to 4 cuts it only to
154. The curve bends at **k = 3**, which also matches the three groups we saw
in Task 2.

## Task 4: k-means with k = 3, and the profile table

```{r task4}
# k-means on the standardized columns; nstart = 20 tries 20 random starts
set.seed(123)
km <- kmeans(X, centers = 3, nstart = 20)
df[, cluster := factor(km$cluster)]

# profile each cluster in the ORIGINAL units (dollars, years)
profile <- df[, .(customers     = .N,
                  online_spend  = round(mean(Online_Spend)),
                  instore_spend = round(mean(InStore_Spend)),
                  total_spend   = round(mean(Online_Spend + InStore_Spend)),
                  age           = round(mean(Age), 1),
                  income        = round(mean(Income)),
                  total_all     = sum(Online_Spend + InStore_Spend)),
              keyby = cluster]
# each cluster's share of all the money customers spent
profile[, share_of_spend_pct := round(100 * total_all / sum(total_all), 1)]
profile[, total_all := NULL]
knitr::kable(profile, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
             col.names = c("Cluster", "Customers", "Online spend (dollars)",
                           "In-store spend (dollars)", "Total spend (dollars)", "Age",
                           "Income (dollars)", "Share of all spend (%)"))

ggplot(df, aes(x = Online_Spend, y = InStore_Spend, color = cluster)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("1" = "#990000", "2" = "#0072B2", "3" = "#E69F00")) +
  labs(title = "The Same Customers, Colored by K-Means (k = 3)",
       x = "Online spend ($)", y = "In-store spend ($)", color = "Cluster") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

- Describe each cluster with the numbers from the profile table, and give
  each one a name a marketer would use.
- Why is the profile table computed on the original columns (`df`) and not
  on the standardized ones (`X`)?

**Answer:** Cluster 1, **in-store loyalists**: 68 customers who spend
\$2,453 in the stores and only \$418 online; the oldest group (46 on
average), income \$59,542. Cluster 2, **young online shoppers**: 67 customers
who spend \$1,185 online and \$306 in the stores; age 25, income \$35,594,
the lowest. Cluster 3, **omni-channel big spenders**: 63 customers who spend
about \$2,000 in each channel, \$4,074 in total; age 35, the highest income
at \$79,161. The profile uses the original columns because "\$2,453 in the
stores" means something to a manager, and "1.2 standard deviations above
average" does not.

## Task 5: what if we had not standardized?

```{r task5}
# the same k-means, on the raw columns (no scale())
set.seed(123)
km_raw <- kmeans(feat, centers = 3, nstart = 20)
df[, cluster_raw := factor(km_raw$cluster)]

raw_profile <- df[, .(customers     = .N,
                      online_spend  = round(mean(Online_Spend)),
                      instore_spend = round(mean(InStore_Spend)),
                      age           = round(mean(Age), 1),
                      income        = round(mean(Income))),
                  keyby = cluster_raw]
knitr::kable(raw_profile, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
             col.names = c("Raw cluster", "Customers", "Online spend (dollars)",
                           "In-store spend (dollars)", "Age", "Income (dollars)"))

# where did each customer go? Rows: the raw clusters from this task.
# Columns: the standardized clusters from Task 4. Each cell counts the
# customers who are in both.
where <- as.data.frame.matrix(table(df$cluster_raw, df$cluster))
colnames(where) <- paste("Task 4 cluster", colnames(where))
rownames(where) <- paste("Raw cluster", rownames(where))
knitr::kable(where, align = "c",
             caption = "Number of customers in each raw cluster (rows) and each Task 4 cluster (columns)")
```

- What separates the three raw clusters? Look at the income column.
- Use the last table (where each customer went): which Task 4 cluster gets
  split or mixed up? Which
  clustering would you hand to the marketing team?

**Answer:** The raw clusters are **income bands**: average incomes of
\$36,117, \$61,931, and \$85,681. Income has the biggest numbers, so it
dominates the distance, exactly as Task 1 warned. The spend patterns get
blurred: raw cluster 1 mixes 59 in-store loyalists with 19 omni-channel
spenders, and raw cluster 3 is mostly the young online shoppers (66) plus 8
others. Only the standardized version recovers the three groups we can see
in Task 2, so that is the one for the marketing team.

## Task 6: the PCA map

```{r task6}
# PCA on the four columns, standardized inside prcomp()
pca <- prcomp(feat, center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)
knitr::kable(round(summary(pca)$importance, 2))

# loadings: how much each column counts in PC1 and PC2
knitr::kable(round(pca$rotation[, 1:2], 2))

# the map: every customer at its (PC1, PC2), colored by cluster, plus the arrows
scores   <- data.table(pca$x[, 1:2], cluster = df$cluster)
loadings <- data.table(pca$rotation[, 1:2], variable = rownames(pca$rotation))
arrow_scale <- 2.5

ggplot() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey70") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey70") +
  geom_point(data = scores, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = cluster),
             size = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_segment(data = loadings,
               aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = PC1 * arrow_scale, yend = PC2 * arrow_scale),
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm")), linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_label(data = loadings,
             aes(x = PC1 * arrow_scale * 1.3, y = PC2 * arrow_scale * 1.3,
                 label = variable), size = 4, fill = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("1" = "#990000", "2" = "#0072B2", "3" = "#E69F00")) +
  labs(title = "PCA Map of the 198 Customers",
       x = "PC1", y = "PC2", color = "Cluster") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

- How much of the variation do PC1 and PC2 keep together? (The
  "Cumulative Proportion" row of the first table.)
- Read the loadings: what does it mean to move **right** on PC1? To move
  **down** on PC2? (PCA picks the direction of each axis arbitrarily; only
  the arrows tell you what the axes mean.)
- Where does each cluster sit on the map? Do they separate?

**Answer:** Together they keep **89%** of the variation (PC1 56%, PC2 34%),
so this two-axis map is almost the whole story. PC1 loads on in-store spend
(0.63), age (0.58), and income (0.50): moving right means **older, richer,
and spending more in the stores**. PC2 loads negatively on online spend
(-0.81) and income (-0.51): moving **down** means **more online spend and more
income**. The young online shoppers sit on the left; the in-store loyalists
on the right and up; the omni-channel spenders on the right and down, next to
the online-spend arrow. Three clean clouds, the same three groups as Task 4.

## Task 7: the recommendation

- Which segment is the most valuable: per customer, and in total? Use the
  profile table from Task 4.
- Propose **one marketing action per segment**: which channel, which offer,
  which message.
- State **one limitation** of this analysis for those decisions.

**Answer:** The **omni-channel big spenders** are the most valuable on both
counts: \$4,074 per customer, and 46.5% of all the money spent by 32% of the
customers. Actions: (1) omni-channel: protect them with a loyalty program that
works across channels (points earned online, spent in store; early access);
(2) in-store loyalists: in-store service and events, plus an easy first step
online such as buy online, pick up in store; (3) young online shoppers: mobile
and social promotions, free-shipping thresholds that raise the basket; they
spend the least today but have the longest customer lifetime ahead. Limitation:
the clusters **describe** customers, they do not explain them. Nothing here
says that moving a loyalist online would raise their spending; that needs an
experiment. Also, k = 3 is a choice, and spend is one year of history.
